questions.q: When does the current platform's contract or support end, and what happens if you are still on it then?
questions.why: The date sets the pace of everything else.
questions.need: The deadline is known, and the plan finishes before it with margin
questions.how: Put the end date and the cost of overrunning it in the plan

questions.q: What would a failed migration weekend cost, and who would feel it first?
questions.why: Turns risk into a number the business can weigh.
questions.need: The cost of a failed cutover is known, and the plan is shaped around it
questions.how: Agree with the business which applications cannot be down, and for how long

questions.q: How many virtual machines are there, at which sites, and how many have no clear owner?
questions.why: Machines without owners cannot be scheduled or tested.
questions.need: Every virtual machine is known, with an owner
questions.how: Run discovery at every site and assign owners

questions.q: Do you know what each application depends on: databases, file shares, licences, hard-coded addresses?
questions.why: Hidden dependencies are what break a cutover.
questions.need: Every application's dependencies are mapped and confirmed by its owner
questions.how: Map dependencies from traffic, then review them with each owner

questions.q: Have you migrated anything yet, even in test, and what went wrong?
questions.why: A first test finds the problems cheaply.
questions.need: A test migration of a representative group has run and its findings are closed
questions.how: Migrate one representative group in a test window

questions.q: If a cutover fails at 3 a.m., how do you go back, and has anyone tried it?
questions.why: Rollback is the safety net for every wave.
questions.need: Every wave has a rollback that has been tested
questions.how: Write and rehearse the rollback for the first wave

questions.q: Will backup, monitoring and security tools work on the new platform on day one?
questions.why: The platform moves; the tools around it must too.
questions.need: Backup, monitoring and security run on the new platform before the first production wave
questions.how: List every tool that touches the platform and test each on the new one

questions.q: Who decides that a wave is done and the old machines can be switched off?
questions.why: Without an owner, the old platform never goes away.
questions.need: Each wave has an owner who signs it off, and the old machines are switched off on schedule
questions.how: Name a wave owner and agree what done means

questions.q: Which servers and storage arrays must stay in use, and until when are they supported?
questions.why: Reusing hardware already owned can change the cost and the timing of the move.
questions.need: The hardware that stays is known, with its support dates and whether the new platform can use it
questions.how: List servers and arrays with their end-of-support dates, and check each against the new platform's support list

questions.q: How long can each application be down at cutover, and can its data be copied ahead of time?
questions.why: Copying data ahead and cutting over within days keeps the downtime to the last changes; waiting too long makes the copy grow on the source.
questions.need: Each wave copies its data ahead and cuts over within days, inside a window agreed with the application owner
questions.how: Seed each wave's data ahead and plan its cutover within a week

questions.q: Which database servers should be rebuilt on the new platform rather than copied as they are?
questions.why: Moving a database like for like is fast; rebuilding it is the moment to fix versions, layout and licences.
questions.need: Every database server has a decision: move as it is, or rebuild on purpose
questions.how: Review each database server with its DBA and decide move or rebuild
